newsitem.title: USA: Oakland school district upholds black English plan.
newsitem.headline: Oakland school district upholds black English plan.

text.p: Oakland's explosive decision to recognise so-called black English in the classroom has ignited a national furore, but school officials said this week they stand behind their unprecedented language plan.

By recognising black English, otherwise known as Ebonics, as the primary language of many of the district's 28,000 black students, Oakland touched off a heated debate across the United States about race and education that has thrust this otherwise obscure northern California school board into the spotlight.

"We have come under attack ... under a barrage from people all over the world," said Oakland Unified School District spokeswoman Darolyn Davis. "But it's all been a rush to judgment, a knee-jerk reaction based on misinformation."

The controversial resolution, approved last week by the school board, called on the district to provide teacher and parent training in black English language patterns, recognise Ebonics as distinct from standard English and help black students who use Ebonics to master standard English. The term Ebonics was derived from the words ebony and phonics.
Since Oakland took action, the resolution has drawn heavy fire, from officials in Oakland, the state, and prominent black Americans. Even the White House jumped into the fray on Tuesday.
"Elevating 'black English' to the status of a language is not the way to raise standards of achievement in our schools and for our students," Education Secretary Richard Riley said.

California's secretary of child development and education, Marian Bergeson, deemed the policy "deeply troubling." Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson said the school board's decision would undermine black students' chances for success.

The Oakland school board did not think its Ebonics plan would become a racial "flashpoint" for the nation, said incoming board president Jean Quan, who is a Chinese American. "We inadvertently stirred national insecurity," she said.
Oakland's superintendent, Carolyn Getridge, and other school officials insisted this week that their critics did not fully understood their Ebonics policy.

The district said that it will not teach Ebonics in place of standard English and is not trying to classify Ebonics-speaking black students as bilingual in order to "pilfer" federal funds. "The actions of the board of education have been publically misunderstood," it said in a statement.
For several decades black English has been the source of controversy and debate among linguists and educators, but until now has attracted scant public attention.

Many Americans consider black English to be little more than inner-city slang or broken English, district officials complain. "People think that it's just street slang, laziness," said Quan. "They don't acknowledge that the African American community has its own speech patterns."

The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association in Maryland has classified black English as a social dialect with its own lexicon and syntax, said Karen Beverly-Ducker, director of multi-cultural resource services at the association.

English words in Ebonics lose a "d" following a vowel, so "good" becomes "goo", and "th" is sometimes replaced with "f", so "with" becomes "wif." One of its most common characteristics is the absence of the forms of the verb "to be," she said.

In its Ebonics resolution, the Oakland school board goes further than many linguists in describing black English as a distinct language, rather than a dialect of standard English, with roots in West African languages.

The district contends black English is the primary language of many of its black students, who may fall behind in school because the language they use at home and on the streets may be different from the standard English used in the classroom.

By recognising Ebonics, Oakland officials said they hope to improve the way black students are taught to read and write standard English. An estimated 53 percent of Oakland's nearly 52,000 students are black and district officials say they have the lowest average grade point averages in the district.

Despite the outburst of public indignation, Davis, Oakland's spokeswoman, said school board officials stands by their Ebonics policy and would not rescind it. Toni Cook, an outspoken board member, added: "We can agree to disagree."
